title: The Unabomber: Misguided to say the least
summary: Josh and Chuck profile the Unabomber, Ted Kaczynski, who sent bombs over roughly seventeen years, starting with a 1978 Northwestern University security guard injury and ending with the killing of timber lobbyist Gilbert Murray. They cover the FBI task force and the Unabomb name, the Montana cabin arrest, the schizophrenia diagnosis and plea bargain, and the 35,000-word manifesto published in the Washington Post and New York Times in 1995. They explain how his brother David Kaczynski recognized the writing and turned him in, and describe Kaczynski's Harvard participation in Henry Murray's humiliation experiment. The episode opens with tour announcements and ends with a listener mail segment about Mexico City's metro and Aztec ruins. It is not a rerun, though the listener mail mentions one.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail
Harvard in the Making of the Unabomber

segments.title: Tour announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts announce Australia and New Zealand tour dates in September with ticket info at sykLive.com, then open the show with banter about Spencer's and Urban Outfitters.

segments.title: 1978 Northwestern bombing and the Unabomber's early victims
segments.summary: Hosts describe the first bomb, opened by Northwestern security guard Terry Marker in 1978, and the Unabomber's indiscriminate targets tied to technology and nature. The gap in victim selection is discussed, including the timber lobbyist killed after a package was addressed to an outdated directory name.

segments.title: Investigation, arrest, and the name Unabomber
segments.summary: The FBI, Postal Service, and ATF formed a task force, and the media coined the name Unabomber. The case became the longest and most expensive FBI investigation at that time. Kaczynski was arrested at his Lincoln, Montana cabin after his brother David turned him in, and FC markings stood for Freedom Club.

segments.title: Plea bargain and schizophrenia diagnosis
segments.summary: Kaczynski tried to kill himself in jail, leading to a psychiatric evaluation and a paranoid schizophrenia diagnosis that set up a plea bargain avoiding the death penalty. He pleaded guilty in January 1998 and received eight life sentences. The hosts discuss doubts about the diagnosis raised in a Harvard-related article by Alston Chase and the defense conflict over insanity.

segments.title: Manifesto content and critique of technology
segments.summary: The hosts summarize the manifesto's critique of the Industrial Revolution, technological dependence, and social control, and its call to violently overthrow the existing system. They note its insightful points but condemn the violence and debate whether he was a rational agent acting out anger or a desire to kill.

segments.title: Publication in the Washington Post and New York Times
segments.summary: Kaczynski mailed the manifesto to the New York Times and Washington Post in June, with a demand to publish or face more killings. The FBI advised publication, and the Post printed it in a special section. The return address belonged to an uninvolved San Jose executive, Boonlong Ho.

segments.title: David Kaczynski recognizes his brother
segments.summary: Linda Patrick read the manifesto and saw similarities to Ted, and David recognized the phrase cool-headed logicians. The family contacted a lawyer's investigator and a criminal profiler, and then the FBI. The brothers' estrangement and their earlier shared Montana land are described.

segments.title: Kaczynski family background and Harvard years
segments.summary: The hosts describe Ted's childhood isolation, his math prodigy status, going to Harvard at sixteen, and the brothers' separation after Ted disowned David. David later became an anti-death penalty activist and friend of Gary Wright, a bombing victim. Ted's Harvard directory entry in 2012 caused embarrassment.

segments.title: Harvard humiliation experiment with Henry Murray
segments.summary: Kaczynski took part as a student in a Harvard experiment led by psychologist Henry Murray, in which undergraduates were interrogated under bright light and humiliated over their beliefs. The hosts say it likely affected him and that he called those years the worst of his life.

segments.title: Disclaimer on violence
segments.summary: The hosts state that they do not agree with the Unabomber's violence or any indiscriminate killing, and point listeners to further information.

segments.title: Listener mail: Mexico City metro and Aztec ruins
segments.summary: Listener Andrea Gonzales from Mexico writes about the Mexico City metro uncovering Aztec ruins, including the Templo Mayor near the Spanish Cathedral. Hosts discuss a possible Mexico City show and ask for listener commute stories. The episode closes with the show's contact information.
